meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: Key metabolic confounders were heavily missing (HbA1c missing in 91.27%, FPG in 33.22%, BMI unspecified in 32.49% to 33.81% across matched groups) and adjusted for using 'unspecified' missing indicator categories. GLP-1 RA users had markedly higher baseline obesity in crude data (BMI 25-39.9: 43.72% vs 23.61% in insulin and 34.37% in metformin) and higher socioeconomic/insurance status, leaving substantial residual confounding by indication, body habitus, and disease severity.

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Restricting the cohort to patients whose cumulative prescriptions were predominantly a single class throughout total follow-up introduces selection based on post-baseline adherence and tolerability, excluding patients who switched therapies due to lack of efficacy or early complications.

findings.title: Conditioning cohort entry on future treatment patterns
findings.mechanism: Requiring patients to maintain predominant monotherapy from baseline to last follow-up conditions on post-baseline survival and tolerability, introducing immortal time and survivorship selection bias.
evidence: GLP-1 RAs, insulin-only, and metformin-only definitions required cumulative prescription of that medication lasting from baseline to last follow-up while other antidiabetic medications accumulated <6 months (Section 2.1)
362,035 outpatients were excluded due to missing prescription data out of 985,278 initially screened (Figure 1)

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Defining mild/moderate adverse symptoms (diarrhea, vomiting, acne, dizziness) as competing risks rather than clinical events or standard censoring complicates hazard estimation.

findings.title: Non-standard definition of competing risk events
findings.mechanism: Treating acute side effects (e.g., diarrhea, acne, dizziness) as competing risk events that censor the subdistribution for major outcomes can distort the hazard functions if these symptoms are directly on the causal pathway or share common causes with the outcome.
evidence: Competing events were defined as activated by incidence of specific acute symptoms, including diarrhea/emesis, dermatitis tetter, acne, dizziness, arrhythmia (Section 2.3)

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: Over 90% of participants were missing baseline HbA1c and roughly a third were missing BMI, education, and fasting plasma glucose, with 362,035 individuals completely excluded due to prescription data gaps.

findings.title: Massive exclusion and missing covariate information
findings.mechanism: High proportion of missing data in registry records can cause substantial bias if missingness is informative or correlated with socioeconomic status and disease monitoring intensity.
evidence: 362,035 of 985,278 outpatients excluded due to missing prescription data (Figure 1)
HbA1c missingness was 91.27% and FPG missingness was 33.22% (Table 1 footnote)

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: Surveillance and detection bias push estimates away from the null because patients initiated on newer injectable therapies (GLP-1 RAs) undergo more intensive clinical and laboratory follow-up than stable metformin users.

findings.title: Diagnostic surveillance bias with regular expression / ICD-10 outcome capture
findings.mechanism: Patients receiving second-line injectable therapies visit clinics and undergo biochemical testing more frequently, inflating the probability of incidental detection of asymptomatic/mild outcomes (e.g., thyroid nodules/dysfunction, acute nephritis, follicular cysts).
evidence: Outcomes identified using ICD-10 and regular expression matching across outpatient and hospitalization text (Table 2S)
GLP-1 RAs group had significantly higher citizen health insurance coverage (75.60% vs 54.96% in metformin) and higher educational attainment (Table 3S)

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Testing more than 20 individual clinical outcomes across two comparator groups and two duration strata without multiplicity correction increases false-positive associations.

findings.title: Multiple outcome testing without formal pre-registered protocol
findings.mechanism: Assessing numerous exploratory outcome definitions without adjustment for multiple comparisons inflates Type I error rates across dozens of evaluated associations (e.g., leukemia, acne, follicular cysts).
evidence: 20 distinct clinical endpoints evaluated across digestive, renal, thyroid, skin, and hematopoietic systems (Table 2S, Section 2.2)

overall.summary: This retrospective cohort study reports increased hazards of multiple adverse outcomes (including pancreatitis, acute nephritis, renal failure, and thyroid cancer) associated with GLP-1 RA use compared to metformin or insulin. The study is at high risk of bias primarily due to severe confounding and selection biases. Over 90% of baseline HbA1c values and over 32% of BMI values were missing and modeled via crude missing-indicator matching categories. Furthermore, defining treatment groups based on long-term adherence/monotherapy over the entire follow-up period introduces conditioning on post-baseline events, while enhanced diagnostic surveillance among patients on newer injectable drugs likely inflated incidental detection of renal, thyroid, and cutaneous outcomes.

duration_gradient.interpretation: Point estimates are larger in the ≥12 months category; however, given that total mean follow-up is only 23.7 months and no lag was applied, reporting massive relative risks for malignancy within 1–2 years indicates protopathic bias, surveillance bias, or residual confounding rather than plausible biological carcinogenesis.

time_related_biases.summary: The study defines exposure groups based on treatment patterns evaluated over the entire follow-up period rather than at cohort entry, introducing conditioning on future events and immortal time bias. Furthermore, the lack of a lag period combined with a mean follow-up under 24 months creates substantial vulnerability to protopathic and detection bias for slow-onset outcomes like cancer.
